meta: Quentin Massys's Portrait of a Man with a Pink, an early Antwerp portrait bought for the Art Institute of Chicago in 1890.
about: The sitter holds a small pink flower in his raised hand, and his left hand rests on the lower edge of the panel. Quentin Massys painted him early in his career. The Art Institute says the stiff pose followed the fashion for half-length portraits, while the modelled face shows the sitter's own character. The pink, or carnation, could stand for marriage or for the incarnation of Christ. In Paris it was sold twice as a work by Holbein. The second sale, in 1890, brought 13,000 francs from Durand-Ruel, who bought it for Charles Hutchinson on behalf of the Art Institute. |||

meta: Georges Rochegrosse's painting of the emperor Vitellius dragged through Rome, his Paris Salon debut of 1882.
about: A half-undressed man in white and red is hauled through a narrow Roman street while the crowd shouts and reaches for him. He is the emperor Vitellius, who held power for only eight months in the Year of the Four Emperors. Georges Rochegrosse shows him being forced down the Gemonian Stairs against his will, with a long dagger held at his throat. Blood stains his clothes. The painting was Rochegrosse's first appearance at the Paris Salon, in 1882.

meta: Robert S. Duncanson's Landscape with Sheep, a soft-toned view inspired by the countryside near his home in Cincinnati.
about: Sheep graze in a grassy clearing with dense trees and large boulders around it, and light breaks through heavy clouds over distant hills. Robert S. Duncanson took his inspiration from the countryside near his home in Cincinnati. The Smithsonian American Art Museum says he painted farmland to show the beauty of nature and its relation to man. It adds that Americans of the nineteenth century, who felt cut off from nature as industry took more land, would have liked such scenes. The colours are soft pinks and yellows. |||

meta: Franz Anton Maulbertsch's loose oil sketch for an altarpiece of the Presentation of Christ in Saint Ulrich, Vienna, c. 1750.
about: Mary and Joseph have brought the infant Jesus to the temple, where the aged priest Simeon cradles him and looks up to heaven. Franz Anton Maulbertsch painted this loose sketch as the preliminary design for an altarpiece in the Church of Saint Ulrich in Vienna. Strong contrasts of light and shadow add drama. The frame is not original. An Austrian craftsman made it in the mid-1700s, and the Cleveland Museum of Art says its florid style suits Maulbertsch's flickering brushwork. |||
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: Sanford Robinson Gifford's 1880 view of the ruined Parthenon, bought by the Corcoran Gallery in 1881 and now in the National Gallery of Art.
about: Fallen marble blocks lie in the grass in front of the ruined Parthenon, whose Doric columns stand against a hazy sky. A small figure in traditional dress walks near them. Sanford Robinson Gifford signed and dated the canvas in 1880. His estate held it until 12 April 1881, when the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington bought it. The National Gallery of Art acquired it in 2014.

meta: Jacopo de' Barbari's 1504 trompe-l'oeil panel of a dead partridge with iron gauntlets and a crossbow bolt, in Munich.
about: A dead grey partridge hangs beside two iron gauntlets with a crossbow bolt passing through them, all painted to look like objects against a wooden wall. Jacopo de' Barbari dated it on a scrap of paper at the lower right, where he also drew a caduceus. Wikipedia calls it one of the earliest still lifes and trompe-l'oeil paintings made in Europe since antiquity. The panel may have been the back or cover of a portrait, or an amusing decoration for a hunting room. It has been in the Bavarian State Painting Collections since 1804.

meta: Hendrick Avercamp's winter scene with skaters near a castle, a round panel owned by the National Gallery in London.
about: Skaters and strollers crowd a frozen waterway beside a brick castle, with snow on the roofs and bare trees in front. Hendrick Avercamp painted the oak panel soon after a harsh winter of the Little Ice Age. Wikipedia calls him the first Dutch painter to specialise in snow scenes. The National Gallery in London acquired the picture in 1891, when it was square. A cleaning in 1983 showed that Avercamp's original was circular and that another artist had added the corners, so the gallery removed them.

meta: Thomas Dewing's 1877 study of a nude boy, painted in Paris while he studied at the Académie Julian.
about: Palm fronds, a smoking censer and an elk-skin rug surround a nude boy who arranges reeds at a stone hearth. Thomas Dewing painted The Sorcerer's Slave in Paris in 1877 while he was studying at the Académie Julian. It is an académie, a full-length study from a live model. The classical stance and the setting recall the mannered bodies and Orientalist themes favoured by Gustave Boulanger and Jules Lefebvre. |||

meta: Antonis Mor's portrait of a young boy with a monkey, whose sitter has long been debated, in Kassel.
about: On a ledge beside a boy in a gold-braided doublet sits a small monkey, and a painted landscape hangs behind them. Antonis Mor's portrait has a disputed history. Older catalogues took the boy for the Spanish infant Don Carlos, and later writers read him as a court jester. No answer has won general agreement. The painting is with Hessen Kassel Heritage. |||

meta: Carlo Maratti's chalk studies of a kneeling woman's drapery and a young woman's head, probably for a Magdalene.
about: A kneeling woman wrapped in a veil and sash fills the centre of the sheet, turned to the left in profile with one arm raised. At the top right is a separate head of a young woman with downcast eyes and curled hair. Carlo Maratti drew them in black and white chalk on blue-grey paper. The Cooper Hewitt thinks they are probably studies for a Magdalene. A drapery study fills the lower right. |||

meta: Ike Taiga's two-panel ink screen of bamboo and rocks as the sky clears after rain, made in the mid-1700s.
about: Rain-swollen water rushes from the mountains into a river, and far off a village sits among giant bamboo. Ike Taiga painted this two-panel folding screen in ink on paper. The title written on it matches one on a design in his book Brush Methods. The Cleveland Museum of Art reads the idea as scenery and spirit refreshed by rain. A flat rock in the foreground works like a platform and invites the viewer to step into the scene. The museum adds that Taiga made over 1,000 compositions in various formats. |||
credit_line: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

meta: Balthasar van der Ast's small Basket of Flowers, a still life of about 1622 given to the National Gallery of Art in 1992.
about: A wicker basket overflows with tulips and roses, and beside it on a grey table lie shells, fruit and a sprig of red currants. Balthasar van der Ast painted it around 1622 on a small panel. The first owner may have been Princess Amalia van Solms, since an inventory of her household from August 1632 seems to list it. It later passed through several sales as a pair with another panel. Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon bought it in 1977, and in 1992 they gave it to the National Gallery of Art.
dimensions:
painted surface: 17.8 x 23.5 cm (7 x 9 1/4 in.)
overall (with additions): 18.4 x 24.4 cm (7 1/4 x 9 5/8 in.)
framed: 38.4 x 43.8 x 3.2 cm (15 1/8 x 17 1/4 x 1 1/4 in.)

meta: Pieter Jansz Saenredam's 1640 view of the westernmost bays in the south aisle of the Mariakerk in Utrecht, in the Rijksmuseum.
about: Three men stand and sit near a window, talking, on the checkered floor of a church aisle. Pale vaults rise on tall stone columns above them, and a large Gothic window with tracery lights the space. Pieter Jansz Saenredam painted the south aisle of the Mariakerk in Utrecht. The Rijksmuseum bought the picture at a sale in The Hague in 1885. It was listed there as a work by Van Steenwijk. The price was 46.60 guilders.
